title: Judges 16:15–22
context: Delilah presses Samson day after day until he tells her the truth: he is a Nazirite, and his hair has never been cut. While he sleeps, his head is shaved, and when he wakes he does not know that the LORD has departed from him. The Philistines blind him and set him grinding grain in a Gaza prison. Yet the chapter's quiet note that his hair began to grow again hints that his story is not over.

verses.text: She said to him, “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and have not told me where your great strength lies.”
verses.arminianNotes: "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me?" Arminian readers note Delilah's manipulation, using love as leverage, and Samson's real choice either to see through it or keep yielding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how sin entangles by degrees. Delilah's appeal to love exploits Samson's weakness, and Scripture shows how desire not ruled by God makes a person easy prey for manipulation.

verses.text: When she pressed him daily with her words and urged him, his soul was troubled to death.
verses.arminianNotes: Pressed daily, "his soul was troubled to death." Arminian readers see persistent temptation wearing down resistance, and a warning that continued exposure to sin weakens the will over time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson's lack of self-control has left him defenseless against relentless pressure. They see a picture of the bondage that sin produces when a person keeps returning to it.

verses.text: He told her all his heart and said to her, “No razor has ever come on my head; for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, then my strength will go from me and I will become weak, and be like any other man.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samson tells "all his heart": he has been "a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb." Arminian readers see the moment of real betrayal: Samson gives away the sign of his consecration to buy peace with Delilah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson knew his strength was tied to his separation to God (13:5). His disclosure is a breach of trust with God, the final step in treating his calling as his own possession.

verses.text: When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called for the lords of the Philistines, saying, “Come up this once, for he has told me all his heart.” Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Delilah knows he has told the truth and calls the lords, who arrive with the money. Arminian readers note the grim exchange: Samson's secret is sold, and Delilah's free choice for silver over loyalty is laid bare.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the stark detail that the lords "brought the money in their hand." The betrayal is complete, and the text exposes the greed and cruelty at work without softening it.

verses.text: She made him sleep on her knees; and she called for a man and shaved off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him.
verses.arminianNotes: She lulls him to sleep and has his seven locks shaved, and "his strength went from him." Arminian readers see the consequences of sin arriving: a vow broken through Samson's own carelessness, with real loss following.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the hair was the outward sign of consecration, not a magic source. When the sign is violated, God withdraws his empowering, showing that Samson's strength always depended on God.

verses.text: She said, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke out of his sleep, and said, “I will go out as at other times, and shake myself free.” But he didn’t know that the LORD had departed from him.
verses.arminianNotes: "He didn't know that the LORD had departed from him." Arminian readers see a sobering warning: God's empowering presence can be withdrawn after persistent sin, and a person may not even notice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this departure concerns the Spirit's empowering for Samson's office as judge, comparable to 1 Samuel 16:14 with Saul, rather than saving grace. Hebrews 11:32 later names Samson among people of faith.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions see real tragedy and real loss here. Arminian readers often take the verse as a warning that God's presence can be forfeited through persistent sin, and some extend that warning to salvation itself. Reformed readers usually distinguish the Spirit's empowering for office, which can be withdrawn, from regenerating grace, which God preserves. They point to Samson's restored strength and his listing in Hebrews 11:32.

verses.text: The Philistines laid hold on him and put out his eyes; and they brought him down to Gaza and bound him with fetters of bronze; and he ground at the mill in the prison.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines put out his eyes, bind him with bronze fetters, and make him grind at the mill in Gaza. Arminian readers see the bitter fruit of sin: the man led by his eyes now loses them, a sobering moral consequence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reversal: the judge sent to begin delivering Israel is now enslaved in the very city whose gate he carried off. God's discipline is severe, yet it serves his larger purposes.

verses.text: However, the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaved.
verses.arminianNotes: "The hair of his head began to grow again." Arminian readers see a hint of hope: Samson's story is not finished, and the way back to God through humility and repentance remains open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the regrowing hair as a quiet sign that God has not abandoned his purpose. The narrator signals that the Philistines' triumph is not the end, because God's plan through Samson is not yet finished.
